Our study confirms that personalization yields substantial retention gains under perfect gating, yet reveals that accurate gating remains an open and critical challenge. Our benchmark and source code are available at https://github.com/yeonjun-in/PerMemBench.

2605.27879.title: Towards Faithful Agentic XAI: A Verification Method and an Open-World Benchmark for Better Model Faithfulness
2605.27879.authors: Jaechang Kim, Sunung Mun, Seungjoon Lee, Jaewoong Cho, Jungseul Ok
2605.27879.abstract: Explainable AI (XAI) helps users interpret model behavior and identify potential faults. Agentic XAI systems use Large Language Models (LLMs) to make explanations more accessible through natural-language interaction, but they can also produce plausible yet unfaithful explanations. This risk arises because unreliable XAI outputs for complex models can be amplified by LLMs and mislead users. We propose Faithful Agentic XAI (FAX), a verification method that improves the faithfulness of Agentic XAI explanations. FAX decomposes draft explanations into claims and tests them with inherently faithful tools that query the target model directly, filtering unsupported or contradicted claims before final generation. We also introduce CRAFTER-XAI-Bench, an open-world reinforcement learning benchmark with complex policies, diverse goals, and challenging scenarios for assessing model-specific faithfulness. On CRAFTER-XAI-Bench, FAX improves simulation faithfulness from 0.20 for the strongest baseline to 0.46 while maintaining high informativeness, relevance, and fluency. On three tabular benchmarks, FAX performs competitively with prior Agentic XAI baselines, but our analysis shows that these settings can conflate task accuracy with model-specific faithfulness. These findings show that explicit verification is essential for faithful Agentic XAI and that faithfulness benchmarks must be designed to test explanations against the behavior of the target model itself.

2606.06462.title: Benchmark Everything Everywhere All at Once
2606.06462.authors: Shiyun Xiong, Dongming Wu, Peiwen Sun, Yuang Ai, Bokang Yang, Wencheng Han, Xiao-Hui Li, Xiangyu Yue
2606.06462.abstract: Benchmarks provide standardized measures for evaluating and advancing large language models (LLMs) and multimodal LLMs (MLLMs). As models improve, existing benchmarks can approach saturation, making it harder to challenge models and distinguish among them. While reusing annotated datasets can reduce data collection and labeling effort, constructing new benchmarks remains labor-intensive, and existing agent-based approaches often target specific tasks or automate only parts of the process. To address these challenges, we introduce BenchHarness, an autonomous harness for end-to-end benchmark customization. It coordinates multiple agents and tools to analyze user requirements, search for suitable datasets, and construct validated benchmarks, with support for refinement based on model performance. To evaluate BenchHarness, we construct 16 benchmarks spanning diverse tasks and modalities. Human review and LLM-as-a-judge assessments indicate high benchmark quality, while evaluations across multiple models reveal challenging tasks and meaningful performance differences. In comparisons with source benchmarks, the generated benchmarks yield lower scores and larger performance gaps, even when the originals approach saturation. BenchHarness thus provides a reusable approach to benchmark construction, supporting informative evaluation as model capabilities and user needs evolve. Our code and benchmarks are publicly available.

2606.11078.title: A History-Aware Visually Grounded Critic for Computer Use Agents
2606.11078.authors: Jaewoo Lee, Zaid Khan, Archiki Prasad, Justin Chih-Yao Chen, Supriyo Chakraborty, Kartik Balasubramaniam, Sambit Sahu, Elias Stengel-Eskin, Hyunji Lee, Mohit Bansal
2606.11078.abstract: Various test-time interventions for Computer Use Agents (CUAs), including critic models, have been developed to improve performance through pre-execution action evaluation in complex Graphical User Interface (GUI) environments. However, existing critics suffer from two key limitations: they (1) focus primarily on short-sighted decision loops (e.g., forgetting earlier actions) and (2) lack the visual grounding needed to detect flawed actions (e.g., clicking wrong UI elements). To address these, we introduce HiViG, a History-aware Visually Grounded test-time framework, built around a multimodal critic trained on real GUI trajectories to abstract past interactions into a compact record and to evaluate actions with visual grounding. At test time, HiViG integrates the critic into the policy decision loop to provide macro-action history, which summarizes the policy's completed achievements, and visually grounded critique, which verifies raw execution coordinates against the current screenshot to intercept errors before execution. Across web, mobile, and desktop benchmarks, HiViG consistently outperforms existing scalar and verbal critics, improving average success rates over the strongest baseline by 5.8% for Qwen3-VL-32B and 9.0% for Gemini-3-Flash, and demonstrates strong cross-platform generalization. Ablations show that macro-action history mitigates short-sighted planning and visually grounded critique reduces execution errors, with both components being critical for test-time scaling in long-horizon GUI tasks.

2607.19355.title: Information Discernment in Large Language Models
2607.19355.authors: Joshua Ashkinaze, Laura Kurek, Alina Faisal, Tongyuan Miao, Mariam Joseph, Ceren Budak, Eric Gilbert
2607.19355.abstract: LLMs are increasingly used with external knowledge sources like the internet. Do they weigh information appropriately -- updating more for reliable sources (source discernment) and more when claims bring priors closer to the truth (truth discernment)? We formalize this as information discernment and introduce Learn2Discern (L2D), an experimental framework and benchmark grounded in three normative axioms with interpretable metrics. To establish external validity, a pre-registered, quota-matched user study (n=299) confirms that real LLM users endorse all three axioms and report that violations reduce their trust and usage intent. Across 13 models and nearly 670K trials, we find consistent failures across both dimensions: models perform near chance on source and truth discernment, rely on source popularity twice as much as source reliability, and update roughly equally whether a claim improves or worsens their position relative to the ground truth. Models integrate external knowledge most effectively on datasets where their priors are already the most accurate. Newer and larger models improve truth discernment but not source discernment, a blind spot that model complexity does not address. We identify simple inference-time interventions that improve both forms of discernment. We release our dataset and survey as a testbed for a core alignment property that scales in importance as LLMs replace traditional search.

2607.23586.title: Are You Still the Agent I Authorized? Earned Authority under a Fixed Ceiling for Evolving Agents
2607.23586.abstract: Long-lived AI agents increasingly evolve after deployment by retaining experience, acquiring skills and tools, revising workflows, delegating work, and moving across task phases. This improves adaptation but creates a distinct authorization problem. Tool-enabled agents can turn model errors and prompt injections into consequential external actions; when evolution occurs under a live grant, the subject exercising that authority or the context in which it acts may no longer match what the user evaluated. Evolution can change both the effects reachable under an old grant and the authority required by the task, which may rise, fall, or become incomparable. Existing tool policies constrain actions but do not determine when a grant survives this change. We formulate authorization continuity: when does an existing grant remain valid, how may active authority change, and what boundary must never move? Our state-bound model fixes a transition envelope and an immutable effect ceiling at grant time. The envelope determines whether the grant survives a mutation; below the ceiling, authority may contract freely and expand only under specified evidence conditions. We distinguish requested from realized effects and prove that, under complete mediation, sound effect abstraction, attenuating delegation, and monitor integrity, mutation cannot amplify protected effects beyond the user-issued ceiling. Agent-produced evidence may allocate authority below the ceiling but cannot raise it. Finally, we map six mutation classes to their authorization consequences.

2608.07437.title: Fisher-R1: Training LLM Agents for Reliable Hypothesis Testing
2608.07437.authors: Jiacheng Miao, Jin Mu, Guanhua Chen, James Zou
2608.07437.abstract: Reliable hypothesis testing is the foundation of many empirical scientific claims. Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly used to automate this process, as they can inspect datasets, generate code, and produce analyses end-to-end. However, we show that they frequently make subtle inferential errors that lead to incorrect conclusions despite correctly executed analyses. Existing benchmarks fail to capture this failure mode, as they rarely assess whether a reported p-value is statistically valid given the assumptions underlying the data. We address this gap by building P-Bench, a benchmark comprising 425 open-ended, realistic hypothesis-testing tasks spanning economics, biology, and medicine. Each task requires an agent to select a statistical method, compute a p-value, and draw a conclusion given only a scientific hypothesis and a dataset. We further introduce Fisher-R1, an open-weight LLM agent trained for rigorous hypothesis testing using synthetic tasks and reinforcement learning. On P-Bench, Fisher-R1-14B substantially improves over its backbone and outperforms strong proprietary and open-source baselines, including GPT-5.4 and DeepSeekV4-Pro, achieving a 21% average relative improvement in single-trial success over DeepSeek-V4-Pro, with gains up to 26% on the most challenging tasks. Our results demonstrate that current LLM agents lack reliable statistical reasoning for hypothesis testing and that reinforcement learning on tasks with verified statistical reward substantially improves reliability.

2609.06960.title: iBrain: A Unified Foundation Model Reading the Brain from Surface to Spikes
2609.06960.authors: Ying Chen, Tiou Wang, Zhifeng Yue
2609.06960.abstract: Invasive neural recordings provide high-fidelity measurements of brain activity, with signals such as intracranial EEG (iEEG) and intracortical spiking activity capturing neural dynamics at different spatial and temporal scales. Yet existing neural foundation models have largely been developed independently for different invasive recording paradigms, leaving joint pretraining across heterogeneous invasive signals underexplored. In this work, we introduce iBrain, a unified foundation model that jointly learns from iEEG and spiking activity. iBrain employs signal-specific encoders to accommodate their distinct signal characteristics and a shared spatiotemporal Transformer backbone to model dependencies across recording channels and time. We pretrain iBrain on over 7,000 hours of heterogeneous neural recordings using masked signal reconstruction and channel-view alignment, promoting contextual modeling of neural dynamics and robustness across different channels. iBrain consistently outperforms single-signal pretraining baselines and achieves state-of-the-art performance on multiple benchmarks. Further experiments demonstrate that iBrain exhibits transferability and data efficiency across diverse recording settings. These results highlight the potential of joint pretraining on heterogeneous invasive neural recordings to support scalable neural modeling and transferable representations across recording settings and downstream tasks.

2609.33699.title: SpecRead: A Benchmark for Measuring Whether Language Models Understand Hardware Specifications
2609.33699.abstract: Existing benchmarks for large language models (LLMs) in hardware design evaluate downstream artifacts such as generated RTL, assertions, or testbenches. When a model fails, it may have misread the specification or understood it and failed to write the code. We present SpecRead, a benchmark that isolates specification comprehension from generation ability. SpecRead v2.2 contains 383 questions over 10 open-source OpenTitan IP blocks in four types: exact retrieval, cross-section reasoning, contradiction detection in mutated specifications, and spec-RTL consistency checking, plus 41 distractor controls and 41 consistent-RTL controls. Type-4 items use real RTL mutations retained only when Icarus Verilog simulation shows a behavioral change. A with-spec vs. without-spec ablation suggests the questions require the excerpt rather than training recall alone, though it does not rule out memorization of the unmutated source text helping a model spot mutations. Ministral-3B scores 33.7% overall (129/383). On t3, verdict-plus-location accuracy is 48.0% with a 51.2% distractor false-positive rate. On t4, the violation-vs.-compliant decision is effectively degenerate (MCC -0.06, balanced accuracy 49.5%), flagging all 41 consistent-RTL controls; location accuracy remains measurable at 79.2%. Layered scoring suggests, as a hypothesis, that the fine-grained violation taxonomy is the hard part, though the category labels are not independently validated. A rule-table prompting intervention on a 60-question sample lowers accuracy on every type except t2 (tied). SpecRead is automatically scorable by deterministic checks, with gray-zone cases counted wrong under the conservative main scoring, regenerable for type-3 items via mutation injection, and built exclusively from public sources.

2609.35149.title: Agent Calibration under Deployment Change: Acceptance Contracts, Trajectory Repair, and Adaptation Costs
2609.35149.authors: Yaxiao Liu (PwC China AI Center), Pengbo Liu (PwC China AI Center), Yiwen Liu (PwC China AI Center), Yihua Guan (PwC China AI Center), Xingjian Li (PwC China AI Center), Jiaxing Song (Tsinghua University)
2609.35149.abstract: An agent can remain operational after a model, tool, or user-context change while losing capabilities required at its destination. We define agent calibration as qualification against a versioned deployment contract. The contract specifies basic capabilities and end-to-end reachability, technical and professional precision, and acceptance by intended users. For each requirement, a source-to-destination map records what must be preserved, transformed, added, or retired. Experts supply benchmarks, positive and negative examples, annotated trajectories, and cost limits. These instruments guide changes to prompts and context, tool calls and other harness settings, or an external compact policy while the foundation model remains frozen. Candidate revisions are evaluated against fixed acceptance criteria using independent evidence. We compare the costs of maintaining a harness with and without an external policy, including annotation, training, serving, review, and rework. Three diagnostic audits illustrate the limits of aggregate scores. On a 100-item intent task, each model solved cases the other missed. In a 60-record synthetic financial reporting fixture, five records passed a numeric proxy but failed the reporting contract. In a target-only WebMall snapshot, quota interruptions affected 132 of 171 attempts. These observations motivate paired reruns, checkpoint replay, and separate measurement of repaired and newly failed cases. We specify controlled experiments to test whether calibration increases accepted deliveries at a given cost.

2609.35744.title: FinAutoRubric: Expert-Guided Automatic Rubric Generation for Evaluating Financial Research Agents
2609.35744.authors: Hoyoung Lee, Suyeol Yun, Jack Haverty, Yunju Cho, Meesong Kim, Daekyung Park, Sumin Kim, Jihoon Kwon, Jasmine Jia Geng, Andrew Chin, Yin Luo, Edward Tong, Yu Yu, Zach Golkhou, Minkyu Kim, Igor Halperin, Young Cha, Alejandro Lopez-Lira, Chanyeol Choi, Yongjae Lee
2609.35744.abstract: Evaluating finance research agents requires rubrics that reflect expert standards and fix the values correct as of an information cutoff. Expert-reviewed finance benchmarks rely on fixed, per-item rubrics, which are costly to extend and cannot encode each institution's own standard. In FinAutoRubric, experts specify reusable evaluation guidance, while agents and code carry out query-specific rubric generation, review, and validation. This expert guidance governs every agent, as prompts and as rules that code enforces, and a Task Bank of reusable criteria carries it across tasks. In long-horizon loops that follow the expert guidance, a writer agent researches every expected value and a reviewer agent verifies it, and failures escalate to a human. On three expert-authored finance benchmarks, its rubrics track expert scoring as closely as the strongest evaluated generator while stating the expert rubric's expected value for more criteria, their scores agree with human grading, and in-house analysts prefer them in a blind review. The released 100-query FinAutoRubric Benchmark, built from in-house analysts' key questions across 78 tasks and eight asset classes, shows that rubrics from an earlier model generation still leave headroom for a later one.

2609.37054.title: ACTR: Aligning Thoughts and Responses for Multilingual Safety in Reasoning LLMs
2609.37054.authors: Xianhui Zhang, Jian Yu, Chengyu Xie, Chenhang Cui, Shuyi Miao, Pengyang Shao, Yu Zheng, Fei Shen, Tat-Seng Chua
2609.37054.abstract: Ensuring the safety of reasoning large language models (LLMs) across languages is essential for their reliable deployment. However, when exposed to jailbreak attacks in non-high-resource languages, these models may generate unsafe responses even when their reasoning traces identify safety risks. To address this issue, we propose aligning cross-lingual thoughts and responses (ACTR), a framework that improves multilingual safety alignment by strengthening the use of existing safety reasoning. Specifically, we first present the think gap score (TGS) to compare the normalized contributions of reasoning traces to attention outputs during response generation across languages, and use reasoning- trace substitution to measure the cross-lingual safety gap. Next, using a corpus of jailbreak queries, we assess neuron importance through changes in response representations caused by neuron masking and compare the high-importance neuron sets obtained with reasoning enabled and disabled to identify safety think neurons that support the use of safety reasoning. Finally, we devise neuron-selective consistency optimization (NSCO), which uses a frozen judge model to reward agreement between the safety categories of reasoning traces and responses while updating only the parameters associated with the selected neurons, requiring no human-annotated responses or preference data. Across two reasoning models, ACTR achieves lower average attack success rates than the evaluated state-of-the-art methods on AdvBench-X and MultiJail, with safety gains extending to unseen languages, while preserving or improving average performance on multilingual knowledge and mathematical reasoning tasks and limiting false refusals of benign requests. Warning: this paper contains examples with unsafe content.

2610.00636.title: CompMat-Bench: Benchmarking AI Agents for Computational Materials Science
2610.00636.authors: Chenmu Zhang, Levi Felix, Jun-Jie Zhang, Xingfu Li, Xuelian Jiang, Tao Jiang, Subhendu Mishra, Xixi Qin, Boris Yakobson
2610.00636.abstract: Evaluating AI agents on scientific research tasks is constrained by the time and resources required for the underlying experiments or calculations. In computational materials research, repeating the same expensive simulations across agents and trials can make evaluation impractical. We introduce CompMat-Bench, a benchmark of 94 tasks derived from recently published computational materials studies, each asking agents to complete a step toward achieving the study's scientific goal. We reproduce the research steps in advance and assess agents on preparing inputs and analyzing outputs for expensive simulations, so expensive simulations can be avoided during evaluation. The reproduced inputs and results serve as ground truth for grading agents with fixed rules, without an LLM judge. We extend the benchmark to four evaluation conditions: single tasks and workflows composed of related tasks, each with full or reduced methodological guidance. In a workflow, the agent runs all simulations itself. With full guidance on single tasks, agents based on nine LLMs demonstrate the ability to complete individual materials research steps, with pass rates of 62.8-97.9% across 94 tasks. Both longer workflows and reduced guidance can limit agent performance, but in different ways for different agents: they lower the pass rates of the weaker agents, whereas the stronger agents fall only when a long workflow is combined with reduced guidance. Failure analysis attributes more failures to scientific errors than to errors in software usage. CompMat-Bench provides a basis for comparing agents on the steps of real materials research and for analyzing agent failure modes.

2610.06917.title: FluidPD: In-Place Elasticity for SLO-Aware Prefill-Decode Disaggregated LLM Serving
2610.06917.authors: Kartik Ramesh, Kaidi Fu, Zihan Zheng, Yi Zhao, Jiahuan Yu, Fabio Oliveira, Carlos H. A. Costa, Minjia Zhang
2610.06917.abstract: Prefill-decode (P/D) disaggregation serves the two phases of LLM inference on separate workers, typically with a fixed prefill/decode worker ratio. Real workloads exhibit both short bursts and sustained shifts in the prefill-to-decode demand ratio, so a fixed split can violate latency SLOs while capacity sits idle in the other pool. Autoscaling adds capacity, but it reacts slowly, requires spare GPUs, and does not address short-timescale phase imbalance. We present FluidPD, a P/D-disaggregated serving system with SLO-aware in-place elasticity. FluidToken absorbs transient imbalance by offloading a bounded portion of prefill computation to decode workers that have slack. FluidRole absorbs sustained imbalance by switching running workers between the prefill and decode roles in place, without model reload or engine restart. Both are guided by indices that expose the pressure in each phase before it causes SLO violations. On workloads derived from production Azure traces and ShareGPT conversations with sustained shifts in the prefill-to-decode demand ratio, FluidPD improves overall SLO attainment by up to 47.9 percentage points over the best static P/D split for each load, without additional workers.

2610.09335.title: SearchWorld: Spatial Value-Grounded Imagination for UAV Object Search via World Models
2610.09335.authors: Yatai Ji, Zhengqiu Zhu, Yong Zhao, Yue Hu, Fanglong Yao, Chen Gao, Pengfei Zhu, Quanjun Yin
2610.09335.abstract: Autonomous unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) object search involves a closed loop of perception, decision-making, and action under partial observability. Urban environments pose several challenges: large search areas and narrow egocentric views limit coverage, dense 3D geometry constrains safe motion, and open-world instructions require identifying a specific target among distractors. Many existing methods mitigate partial observability through explicit maps or memory representations, yet remain largely reactive, reasoning over past observations without explicitly predicting future states. World models enable prospective reasoning through imagined rollouts. However, image-generating world models can incur high inference latency, while spatially grounded planning remains challenging for latent world models. We propose SearchWorld, a recurrent state-space world model that connects explicit spatial memory with value-guided imagination. The model maintains BEV exploration and obstacle memory and decodes a task-aware spatial value layer to guide search. A cognition-action network uses this learned spatial value prior to improve the policy through imagined rollouts, without training a separate scalar critic. Training progresses from world-model learning to expert imitation and imagination-based exploration refinement. On UAV-ON, SearchWorld improves the success rate to 23.8% (19.5% for the strongest published agent) and raises oracle success to 35.5%, while remaining robust on unseen scenes (19.9% success rate). By grounding imagination in explicit spatial representations, SearchWorld enables UAV agents to plan prospectively rather than react.

2610.09937.title: Where Can a Decision Model Diagnose HVAC Faults? Reasoning Demand, Physical Representation, and Robustness Under Shift
2610.09937.abstract: Artificial intelligence supports building operations in several forms, each with its own barrier. Expert rules must be tuned for every system, supervised models need labeled data that buildings rarely record, and language models return free text that requires human-in-the-loop checking, since their stated confidence is unreliable. A newer kind of pretrained model, here called a decision model, returns a probability for every allowed answer, so one model could serve many decisions without training. This study answers three open questions for fault diagnosis in heating, ventilation, and air-conditioning systems: which decisions such a model can make, what input it needs, and whether its probabilities hold when conditions change. On 128 fault days from four public datasets of real equipment, faults are graded by the reasoning their diagnosis demands, with data given raw, as physical features, or with Brick topology. The decision model Jev, open language models, and a supervised model face nine tests that change season, control configuration, or building. Given physical features, Jev and the larger open model diagnosed faults whose evidence one feature carries, but not faults that need operating context. Under shift they kept their accuracy and calibration, while the supervised model lost 0.33 macro-F1 yet led or tied within a building. Their probabilities still needed correction, and detection was weak. The study maps which faults a decision model can diagnose and from what input, and supports a division of work in which code computes the physics and the model ranks candidate faults for an operator.

2610.17584.title: RAN-JEPA: An Action-Conditioned World Model for Energy-efficient Mobile Network Control
2610.17584.authors: Binghan Wu, Kai Zeng, Kai Yang, Ya-Qin Zhang, Joseph Sifakis, Ye Ouyang
2610.17584.abstract: Operational mobile networks are rich in observations but poor in interventions: they continuously generate large volumes of passive telemetry, while controlled action--response trajectories remain comparatively scarce and costly to collect. This observation--intervention asymmetry is a central obstacle to building practical world models for RAN control. We address this problem with RAN-JEPA, an action-conditioned world model that separates representation learning from intervention learning. The model first learns a predictive latent representation from observation-only network data, adapts that representation to the target deployment domain, and then learns action-conditioned latent dynamics from controlled sleep/wake trajectories while keeping the encoder fixed. We evaluate RAN-JEPA using public operator performance data for pretraining and a real-equipment four-cell 5G testbed for domain adaptation, post-training, and control. Across four future 15-minute intervals, RAN-JEPA achieves lower action-conditioned prediction error than a GPT-2 world-model baseline and a mechanistic rule, while remaining close to a strong persistence reference. What-if evaluation further shows that the model produces distinct and coherent future trajectories under matched SLEEP and KEEP plans. In closed-loop control, RAN-JEPA consistently supports higher sleep ratios than the two baselines at comparable congestion cost. These results show that observation-first, action-conditioned learning can turn abundant passive telemetry and limited intervention data into a practical predictive model for energy-aware RAN control.

2610.23670.title: OwlSight: A Panoramic Monitor for Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
2610.23670.authors: Lewen Yan, Yanxu Zhu, Jie Zhang, Jing Shao
2610.23670.abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) monitoring offers actionable evidence for oversight AI systems, with the potential to enable early detection and intervention. However, existing approaches are focused on specific tasks, whereas the regulation of AI, particularly reasoning models, requires monitoring a broader range of tasks. We introduce Factor for CoT monitoring, a strategy that supports customizing monitoring requirements in the prompt, which enables a single monitor to cover different tasks by relying on different factors. Furthermore, we introduce two types of factors, fine-grained and coarse-grained (e.g., monitoring whether a specific email address has been leaked versus monitoring privacy leakage), to accommodate diverse user monitoring needs. Based on this, we develop a CoT monitor named OwlSight that relies solely on factor to monitor behaviors related to multiple dimensions, including capability, safety, and trustworthiness. Experiments across 15,971 reasoning trajectories show that OwlSight surpasses general-purpose LLMs by 1.32-30.57 and 11.71-27.81 points at fine and coarse granularity, respectively, and achieves state-of-the-art results on OpenAI's CoT monitorability benchmark. It also generalizes to unseen models' CoTs and remains robust to Factor rephrasings, CoT compression, and obfuscation, offering a promising paradigm for CoT monitoring that can contribute to the oversight of frontier AI.

2610.39454.title: Kairos: Fast and Reliable Symbolic Task Planning for Autonomous Robots
2610.39454.authors: Francisco Mart\'in Rico, Esther Aguado Gonz\'alez, Francisco Miguel Moreno Olivo, Rodrigo P\'erez Rodr\'iguez, Jos\'e Miguel Guerrero Hern\'andez, Francisco J. Rodr\'iguez Lera
2610.39454.abstract: Robots that plan while they act need a task planner that reads the models their designers write, answers within milliseconds, and says what each answer means. Models are written in the Planning Domain Definition Language (PDDL), which has grown from classical planning to durative actions, numeric resources, time windows and continuous change, while planners cover one fragment each and differ in what their failures mean. The contribution in artificial intelligence is Kairos, a single planner, not a portfolio of existing planners, that covers the whole language and derives what each answer guarantees from the search that produced it. We prove when the exhaustion of a search shows that no plan exists, and give a relaxation of temporal tasks that proves unsolvability where temporal search cannot. For the compression of durative actions, we give a criterion on the values that actions read, prove that compression is sound, and show that it is not complete, so its failure is never reported as a proof. An independent validator checks every plan. The engineering application is on-line task planning for robots: Kairos is open source, packaged for the Robot Operating System, and the default planner of a widely used planning framework. On 1,756 public tasks from nine suites, Kairos solves more tasks than the strongest evaluated planner of each suite within 100 milliseconds, 1 second and 30 seconds; it proves ten of eleven unsolvable tasks, and handles each of the seventeen language features probed, where no other planner handles more than eight.

2610.41183.title: Researcher-in-the-Loop Evolutionary Discovery of Entanglement-Assisted Quantum Code Families
2610.41183.authors: Jae-Hyun Baek, Byung-Sun Won, Jon-Lark Kim
2610.41183.abstract: LLM-guided program evolution can produce mathematical constructions, but validity, generality, and reproducibility require distinct evidence. In this paper, we develop a researcher-in-the-loop discovery pipeline combining program evolution, exact evaluation, mathematical generalization, and independent verification. We apply it to entanglement-assisted quantum error-correcting codes (EAQECCs). Evolved programs produced finite qubit constructions from specifications that supplied no family formula. Researcher-directed analysis with a language model led to a general construction and proof drafts, which the researchers revised and checked. The resulting family $[[n,1,n-1;n-q-1]]_q$ exists for prime powers $q\ge3$ at $n\ge2q+1$ and for $q=2$ at odd $n\ge5$; Lean checks its formalized algebraic core. With entanglement lifting, it closes 54 listed table gaps. The evidence includes 115 verified code records, ten DRAT-checked nonexistence results, family implementations and preserved search programs. Controlled studies test how research proposals interact with program generation. Under a mutation-and-restart proposal, iterative evolution improves normalized success-curve area in all ten paired runs and raises success at excluded lengths $n=13,15$ from 13.4% to 62.5% and from 0.9% to 33.4%, respectively. The benefit depends on the proposal. Selected programs combine the proposed moves with objective and restart-counter changes. The pipeline connects finite computational discoveries to a proved family and independently checkable constructions.

2611.04241.title: AceAction-5M: Hierarchical Goals for Generalist Action Learning Across 3D Game Worlds
2611.04241.authors: Ruoxuan Zhang, Kailing Li, Zheyuan Zhou, Boyang Chu, Yingshan Lei, Hongxia Xie, Liang Du, Zixun Sun
2611.04241.abstract: Video games provide a practical setting for collecting vision-language-action (VLA) data, whose acquisition in physical environments is costly. Existing datasets, however, remain limited by restricted game coverage, sparse language supervision, or temporal hierarchies that do not necessarily reflect changes in task objectives. We introduce AceAction, a dataset of human gameplay across multiple 3D games for learning skill composition and subgoal transitions. AceAction organizes demonstrations around complete tasks, linking overall instructions, ordered subgoals, and local skill instructions to temporally aligned visual observations and keyboard-and-mouse actions. To construct these annotations, we develop a vision-language model pipeline that identifies subgoals from changes in objectives or interaction targets, anchors navigation goals to visually recognizable waypoints, and composes adjacent subgoals into task instructions. The resulting demonstrations cover navigation, reconnaissance, combat, interaction, and recovery, with explicit stage boundaries that connect task progression to fine-grained control. We assess annotation quality through model-based verification and human inspection. An audit of 500 trajectories yields a 95.8% pass rate across independent reviewer assessments. AceAction provides a data foundation for studying how agents execute, combine, and switch skills to follow complex instructions in dynamic game environments.

2611.06732.title: ConceptARC at Scale: Studying Conceptual Understanding in Reasoning Models
2611.06732.authors: Philipp Mondorf, Adrien Deli\`ege, Solim LeGris, Claas Beger, Ryan Yi, Barbara Plank, Brenden M. Lake, Todd M. Gureckis
2611.06732.abstract: Large reasoning models (LRMs) perform well on challenging benchmarks, yet it remains unclear whether they form generalizable abstractions across conceptually related reasoning tasks. The Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus (ARC) provides a controlled testbed for studying abstraction, requiring solvers to infer transformation rules over two-dimensional grids from a small set of examples. While ARC evaluates rule abstraction within individual tasks, different tasks may share higher-level structure despite requiring different transformations$\unicode{x2014}$for example, several tasks may involve reasoning about objects contained within other objects. Benchmarks such as ConceptARC capture this structure by grouping ARC-style tasks into recurring spatial and semantic concepts, but they often contain only a few manually constructed tasks per concept. We introduce ConceptARC at Scale, a generator for creating thousands of ARC-style tasks targeting a specific concept. Using this generator, we construct ConceptARC-100, a dataset of 1,600 new, manually reviewed tasks, with 100 tasks for each of the 16 concepts defined by ConceptARC$\unicode{x2014}$ten times the size of the original benchmark. We evaluate a range of recent LRMs and models trained from scratch on ConceptARC-100 to characterize which concepts they solve reliably and where they struggle. We further analyze the models' internal representations and find clear semantic structure: task representations cluster according to the operations applied to objects, such as recoloring, removal, or translation, even when realized through substantially different rules and scenarios. Together, our results suggest that models form stable abstractions of transformation operations that generalize across diverse tasks.

2611.11658.title: Measuring Generative AI Content in Political Campaigns: Evidence of Rising Adoption and Non-Disclosure
2611.11658.authors: Anna-Maria Gueorguieva, Sarah Tran, Nic Weber
2611.11658.abstract: The use of generative AI in political campaigns has drawn public concern and policy attention. Public concerns range from distrust of candidates to skepticism about the authenticity and accuracy of political advertising, including AI-generated images and video. Nearly half of U.S. states have enacted laws that prohibit, or require disclosure of, "materially deceptive" AI-generated content (AIGC) in elections to guard against these concerns. This study measures how candidates and their campaigns produce and circulate AIGC during an election cycle. We develop two measures that estimate not only wether campaigns use AIGC, but how much they produce (magnitude) and in what forms (modality). We apply these measures to a novel dataset of text and images from the campaign websites, X accounts, and emails of 12,977 candidates for U.S. political office from 2023 to 2025. We report three findings. First, detectable AIGC from campaigns increased significantly across modalities over the observation window, and campaigns that use AIGC frequently do not disclose it. Second, incumbents' campaigns produced significantly less AIGC than challengers' campaigns. Third, candidates in states with AIGC disclosure or prohibition laws do not produce measurably less AIGC than candidates in other states. Our method and findings have implications for transparency and trust in elections, and on state laws that regulate AI use in campaigns. Because current state laws largely target mainly "materially deceptive" content, we identify additional policy mechanisms that could increase electoral transparency and improve trust as AIGC becomes more prevalent.

2611.13487.title: The WoW: A Large-Scale World Knowledge Corpus for Full-Lifecycle LLM Training
2611.13487.authors: Tianze Sun (Harbin Institute of Technology), Yongyao Duan (OpenCSG), Sam Chen (OpenCSG), Yuanjian Xu (Hong Kong University of Science and Technology)
2611.13487.abstract: Existing Chinese educational corpora often suffer from fragmented coverage and a lack of systematic organization. In this paper, we propose WoW (\textbf{Wo}rld Kno\textbf{w}ledge), a large-scale dataset designed for the full-cycle training of foundation models. The construction of this dataset is driven by an Educational Knowledge Graph, which serves as a taxonomic backbone for the systematic collection and completion of missing educational modules across all levels. Compared to previous versions, this iteration provides enhanced systematicity, superior quality, and a larger scale, while incorporating multimodal signals and supporting every stage of model development. Experiments demonstrate that WoW significantly improves model performance across diverse benchmarks. To facilitate community research, we further provide an interactive platform for graph-based data selection and retrieval.

2611.14949.title: RSI-PDEbench: A Benchmark for Self-Improving Agents in PDE Solving
2611.14949.authors: Binghang Lu, Lang Cao, Changhong Mou, Yige Sun, Cindy Xiangrui Kong, Zheyuan Deng, Tian Yuan, Bing Hu, Runyu Zhang, Na Lu, Guang Lin
2611.14949.abstract: Identifying and solving partial differential equations (PDEs) from sampled solution data often requires substantial expert effort in equation discovery, coefficient estimation, and numerical solver configuration, especially under noise and distribution shifts. Can large language model (LLM) agents automate this workflow accurately and efficiently? To investigate this question, we introduce RSI-PDEbench, a benchmark of 1,001 cases spanning 42 equation templates, including both classical and fractional PDEs. It provides three evaluation settings: Full evaluates performance on noise-free solution data; Noisy tests robustness to Gaussian noise with an RMS equal to 50\% of the clean-signal RMS; and Hard-OOD tests challenging out-of-distribution generalization to unseen equation templates and shifted coefficient ranges. We further introduce RSI-PDE, a recursively self-improving agent harness that shortlists candidate equations by residual loss, uses relative $L^2$ feedback to refine coefficients and numerical solvers, and applies a validation gate to policy and memory updates. We compare RSI-PDE with single-run baselines and native agent harnesses (Claude Code or Codex) across four frontier models. Across the three settings, RSI-PDE improves the pass rate averaged across the four models by 106.5--181.9\% relative to single-run baselines and by 3.0--19.6\% relative to native harnesses, while reducing total recorded model calls by 46.9\% across the 12 model--setting pairs. These results highlight the potential of validated recursive self-improvement in LLM agents to advance scientific computing.

2611.15215.title: $\varepsilon$-WM: Error-Driven Dynamics Adaptation across Fast--Slow Timescales for World Modeling
2611.15215.authors: Haoyi Zhang, Qi Zhang, Yunfan Ren, Yi Bin, Lei Zhu, Heng Tao Shen
2611.15215.abstract: A core challenge for world models is adapting to sudden, persistent, yet initially unknown changes in robot dynamics. If the world model fails to adapt, its prediction errors accumulate over the open-loop rollout and ultimately mislead the robot's actions. Existing world models, however, struggle to balance three key requirements for dynamics adaptation: responsiveness, rapidly correcting sudden changes; stability, avoiding lasting model updates from transient disturbances; and persistence, retaining adapted dynamics during the observation-free open-loop rollout. Inspired by multi-timescale predictive coding in the human brain, we propose $\varepsilon$-WM, a world model that adapts to unknown dynamics through error-driven corrections across fast and slow timescales. $\varepsilon$-WM incorporates three novel features: 1) Multiple internal experts (MiE) emulate neural pathway reweighting, each combining a fixed base expert with fast--slow adaptation networks. 2) Fast--slow timescale adaptation captures distinct adaptation dynamics: fast states respond rapidly and decay, whereas slow states accumulate corrections and persist. 3) Predictive correction uses prediction errors to update fast and slow states and reweight experts without gradients. During open-loop rollout, each expert feeds back its own predictions, and $\varepsilon$-WM aggregates their outputs through adaptive weighting. Extensive experiments show $\varepsilon$-WM has a consistently lower multi-step mean error than all ten baselines on six datasets, verifying the effectiveness of each feature.

2611.22374.title: AutoE2E: Don't speak - Language free end-to-end autonomy for L2++ ADAS and L4 Robotaxis
2611.22374.authors: Muhammad Zain Khawaja, Zaynab El Mawas, Ryota Yamada, Gabriela Cordova, Arseni Lysak, Intisar Chowdhury, Bharat Jayaprakash, Apostolos Georgiadis, Shri Harsha Adapala, Jatin Gautam, Christoph Bank, Alejandra Solarte Uscategui, Atanasko Boris Mitrev, Hassan Ali Ansari, Nishad Sahu
2611.22374.abstract: AutoE2E is an open-source end-to-end driving model developed by the Autoware Foundation Robotaxi Working Group. It introduces a temporal bird's-eye-view (BEV) architecture that combines multi-camera perception, HD-map information and route conditioning to predict future vehicle motion. The evaluated model uses a pretrained camera-BEV backbone, temporal feature fusion and a lightweight recurrent trajectory planner. It contains approximately 79.9 million parameters, of which approximately 1.45 million are trainable in the evaluated configuration. The v1.0 release provides model checkpoints, training and evaluation code, and DataModelConsole, a dashboard for visualizing and inspecting model experiments. On the KITScenes validation benchmark, the fine-tuned checkpoint achieves an average displacement error (ADE) of 0.745 m and a final displacement error (FDE) of 2.020 m at a three-second prediction horizon. The paper also reports preliminary real-vehicle research conducted with the Technical University of Munich's EDGAR platform, alongside ongoing collaboration with the Karlsruhe Institute of Technology. AutoE2E v1.0 is an early open research release. Its quantitative evaluation is open-loop, and the model has not yet demonstrated validated closed-loop autonomous driving. The release is intended to provide the autonomous-driving community with an inspectable baseline for further research, experimentation and collaborative development.

2611.23700.title: Auditable Clinical Support with Decision Agents
2611.23700.authors: Tiancheng Bao, Riga Wu, Jan Wienhold, Sebastian Billig, Patrick Winnersbach, Hsuan-Chih Chen, Akis Giannoukos, Jiayang Li, Li Shen, Gary Weissman, Eduardo J. Mortani Barbosa Jr, Dyke Ferber, Jakob Nikolas Kather, Christos Davatzikos, Daniel Truhn, Tianyu Han
2611.23700.abstract: Emergency care requires auditable decisions, but a language-model agent just outputs text. We introduce Decision2Care, a decision agent that generates a probability for every option at each step. It diagnosed 546 emergency admissions across 12 diseases with 86.5% accuracy in a median of 2.2 s; language-model agents reached 86.1 to 91.7% but took more than 90 s. Its drug orders were judged guideline-adherent more often than documented first-day care and with about half as many records, it predicted death as well as three ICU clinicians. In the four cases where it was confident but wrong, we traced each decision to one imaging report. Our study suggests that an agent's work-up can be reviewed like a clinician's, motivating prospective trials.

2611.23702.title: KnowMe Paper Radar: Lightweight Discovery of Promising Papers in the Age of Autoresearch
2611.23702.authors: Zhuo Chen, Jian Wang, Jinjie Gu, Lijun Wu
2611.23702.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are pushing research toward semi-automation: ideas turn into preprints ever faster, and autoresearch pipelines add papers of uneven rigor. When a technique can be overtaken within months, citations arrive too late to tell which new papers deserve reading, so strong work goes unnoticed and newcomers lose their bearings. Yet from the day it appears, a preprint carries the track records of the people and institutions behind it. Established researchers guard their reputations and choose problems and collaborators with research taste, so their involvement tends to raise a paper's quality floor. Building on this signal, we present KnowMe Paper Radar, a lightweight arXiv discovery tool that weights each paper's topical relevance by the reputation its authors and institutions stake on it. Author credit also diffuses by message passing along collaborations to surface rising stars, and institutions are profiled through the researchers they hold in each direction rather than by headcount. In a sealed test on 10,386 new papers, those with an identity-bound author were twice as likely to reach the top tenth of early citations. As its library grows into a scholarly knowledge graph that research agents can query through a command-line interface (CLI), KnowMe also offers a promising literature entry point for future autoresearch and recursive self-improvement (RSI).

2611.27741.title: Can Vision-Language Models Synthesize Executable Game-Playing Programs?
2611.27741.authors: Yao Tong, Jiaxin Qi, Dingyu Zhang, Jianqiang Huang
2611.27741.abstract: Recent advances in vision-language models (VLMs) have endowed multimodal agents with increasingly strong visual perception and long-horizon reasoning capabilities, making VLM-based autonomous game playing feasible. Existing game benchmarks primarily evaluate whether an agent can select appropriate actions from the current visual state across different scenarios and games. However, most of them adopt a step-by-step interaction paradigm where the current visual observation is sent to the agent before each action. In practical deployment, this paradigm introduces two fundamental limitations: the game loop must wait for model inference, making real-time interaction impractical, and repeated VLM calls incur substantial cost. Therefore, we propose PlayScriptBench, a script-based game benchmark that evaluates whether VLMs can synthesize an executable game-playing program from game states. This setting jointly evaluates visual grounding, understanding of game dynamics, long-horizon strategic reasoning, and executable program synthesis, providing a more comprehensive assessment of game-playing agents. To support more tractable evaluation for current general-purpose VLMs, we further introduce a four-stage pipeline --- Explore, Perception, API Construction, and Strategy Composition --- that decomposes controller synthesis into game exploration, state perception, interface construction, and strategic control, enabling agents to progressively construct an executable program. Experiments on 16 games spanning 4 genres show that even strong VLMs struggle on our benchmark, revealing a substantial gap between passive visual game understanding and executable closed-loop game control. These results establish script-based controller synthesis as a complementary direction for benchmarking VLM-based game-playing agents.

2611.28202.title: AutoPILOT: A Visual Agent Harness for Real-Time Gameplay
2611.28202.authors: Mark Zhao, Pengcheng Wang, Rui Yang, Jiarui Yao, Xirui Jiang, Yuxi Chen, Bingxuan Li, Hanyang Chen, Ke Yang, Manling Li, Tong Zhang, Huan Zhang
2611.28202.abstract: Multimodal foundation models can play video games well when the game waits for them, but often fail when it keeps running. We find that much of this gap lies in the harness, which decides what the model sees, what it remembers, and how its outputs become actions over time. Existing harnesses such as VISTA improve the first two, yet turn each model call into at most one action, so the agent acts only as often as its model thinks. We introduce AutoPILOT, which changes the third: in each model call, the model can send a primitive action, start an open-loop macro, or write a closed-loop controller that keeps playing from the screen without further model calls until it hands control back. To evaluate agents in real-time games, we build AFK-Bench, 120 diverse browser games grouped by how they respond to inaction and playable in real time or with the clock paused. With GPT-6.1 Sol under the same budgets, AutoPILOT reaches 68.6% real-time success against 38.3% for VISTA, and on GameWorld it keeps 80.0% in real time while VISTA drops from 84.1% to 42.9%. Its gains hold across closed and open-source models, and it reaches VISTA's final success rate at a fifth of its API cost. Our results suggest that how a harness turns model outputs into actions over time is a central yet underexplored part of agent design, and we hope AutoPILOT and AFK-Bench will serve as a foundation for agents in a world that does not wait.

2611.28356.title: Engram: Multi-Stage Memory for Agentic Tuning of Heterogeneous Models
2611.28356.authors: Huanran Li, Nhat X. T. Le, Kevin De Angeli, Yao Xuan, Alireza Vahdatpour, Djordje Gligorijevic
2611.28356.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents can now tune neural networks, yet without cross-session memory they spend costly trials rediscovering known lessons. Reuse is difficult because production models differ in architecture, training setup and inference budget. We present Engram, a memory system that links past trial outcomes with the hypotheses and rationale behind them and assesses whether this evidence applies to the current model. An online agent curates evidence at the decision points where it is needed: Initial Guidance supplies validated lessons at the start, Session Retrieval supplies related past sessions before each batch of hypotheses is generated, and Trial Candidate Review checks each trial candidate against matching past trials. Between sessions, an offline agent distills validated lessons, making the memory self-improving. On two ads models, Engram reaches the 32-trial result of a no-memory control with 47% fewer trials and also ends with a better model on average.

2611.30281.title: Learning Heterogeneous Reasoning in Large Language Models: From Mode Compatibility to Local Bottlenecks
2611.30281.authors: Sunbowen Li, Dandan Song, Shengkun Ma, Xuanning Cao
2611.30281.abstract: Post-training large language models routinely pools reasoning trajectories from diverse teachers or algorithms, yet it remains unclear whether standard supervised fine-tuning (SFT) can learn such heterogeneous strategies without explicit mode conditioning. We study the learnability and local bottlenecks of heterogeneous reasoning through a formal mixture formulation and controlled experiments. We first formalize the representational compatibility of the optimal autoregressive model with latent reasoning mixtures: the target next-token distribution weights modes by their prefix posteriors and concentrates on a single mode once alternative modes assign negligible likelihood to the prefix. In a verifiable symbolic graph-search environment with paired breadth-first and depth-first search trajectories, no consistent disadvantage is observed for unlabeled mixed SFT relative to homogeneous or labeled baselines under matched token budgets while preserving both modes. Scaling across 0.6B-14B models and data budgets largely eliminates global mode confusion, shifting the primary bottleneck to local state-tracking transitions. Because a local mistake affects the final outcome only when subsequent reasoning is sensitive to that step, we find that only a small fraction of local errors are outcome-determining Critical Reasoning Nodes (CRNs), and that single-step repairs at these nodes rescue failing trajectories across symbolic search and natural language benchmarks whenever the model has sufficient downstream competence to complete the remaining derivation. Our environment is open-sourced at https://github.com/Bowen1911/Symbolic_graph_env.

2611.30545.title: Reproducible by Seed? Not on GPUs: Batch-Dependent Non-Determinism in Text-to-Image Models
2611.30545.authors: Javier Conde, Xiuyuan Qi, Shanshan Liu, Pedro Reviriego
2611.30545.abstract: In text to image AI models, fixing the prompt and the random seed is widely assumed to fix the image. We show that it does not on GPUs. We evaluate six text-to-image models (diffusion and autoregressive) under four numerical precisions and quantizations on three GPU types (RTX A6000, RTX 6000 Ada, and H100 NVL), across up to 100 prompts per set for all six models. For each configuration we compare, with the prompt and seed fixed, the image generated alone with the image generated inside a batch, and we also compare across GPUs. Every replay control reported here is bit-exact, so the variation is not random noise: the execution setting, mainly the batch composition and the GPU, decides the output. The effect is large and model dependent. Structural similarity between the single-image and the batched output falls to 0.580 for an autoregressive model in bf16 and to 0.551 with int8. For a second autoregressive model in bf16 it falls to 0.261 with sampled decoding and to 0.229 with greedy decoding, and for an fp8 diffusion model to 0.68. A diffusion model in bf16 stays close to the batch-1 output (0.96-0.98) but changes every image. In most cases the batched image is a different but equally valid image; in some, such as prompts with digits and counters, it is visibly worse. Cross-GPU differences are of the same order as the batch effect: for one autoregressive model in bf16 compared across two GPU architectures (RTX 6000 Ada versus RTX A6000), no image is bit-identical and the cross-GPU LPIPS (0.355 to 0.383) matches the batch effect within one GPU (0.347 to 0.381). The consequences are direct: seeds do not make results reproducible, benchmarks and image-quality comparisons that mix batch sizes or hardware can be biased, and safety audits and A/B tests on generated images need the serving setup reported.

2611.31301.title: MOZAIC: An Audio-Video Deepfake Benchmark for Telling What Is Fake
2611.31301.authors: Shaina Raza, Mohamed Hafez, Ahmed Y. Radwan, Khalid Elgazzar, Kathryn Hume
2611.31301.abstract: Audio-video (AV) deepfakes can fake the face, the voice, or both. Most benchmarks only ask whether a clip is real or fake, so they cannot show whether a detector relies on the picture, the voice, or encoding traces. We present MOZAIC, a paired benchmark with a 4-way label in which every source clip is released in all four combinations of real or fake video and real or fake audio so each modality contribution can be measured directly. Fakes cover inner-face swapping, whole-frame video diffusion and voice conversion. MOZAIC has 137,745 clips from 15,014 source pairs and four tasks: T1 AV authenticity, T2 manipulation type, T3 identity verification and T4 explanation. We evaluate 12 AV multimodal LLMs (MLLMs), train four detectors and fine-tune MLLMs with LoRA. Overall, the best MLLM reaches only 35.6% on the four-way T1 and catches far more video-only fakes than voice-only fakes (43.6% vs 7.5%). Trained detectors reach 98.4% on T1, and LoRA fine-tuning raises explanation scores (OmniVinci 4.17 to 7.40, Qwen2.5-Omni 4.42 to 6.98), but the best T1 detector falls to 78.3% when the face-swap generator is held out of training, so generalization and explanation remain open. We release the dataset, the compact MOZAIC-SMALL split, the code and the prompts. https://vectorinstitute.github.io/mozaic/

2611.31823.title: GaokaoMathGen: Chinese Gaokao Mathematics Finale Problem Generation Controlled by Latent Reasoning Structures
2611.31823.authors: Qian Chen, Kun Zhu, Zhongyi Wang, Ling Chen
2611.31823.abstract: Generating Chinese Gaokao mathematics finale problems requires controlling not only the included skills, but also the underlying mathematical kernel and solution path. Existing LLM-based methods mainly rely on surface-level specifications, while the realized difficulty of generated problems cannot be determined directly from prompted targets. Therefore, we propose GaokaoMathGen, a framework for Chinese Gaokao mathematics finale problem generation controlled by latent reasoning structures. It extracts standardized latent reasoning structures from seed problems and performs constrained synthesis using skills, methods, a core identity, and a pivot step as structural controls. We further estimate realized difficulty through logical-quality filtering, fixed-solver decoding effort, structural features, and solver-output search signals. Experiments show that semantic normalization improves cross-annotator comparability and that 78.0% of 609 scored candidates pass the logical-quality filter. In a teacher audit of the 60 highest-effort candidates, all were judged to reach finale or penultimate problem difficulty, and only one exhibited a severe logical issue. These results support latent reasoning structures as effective control signals for generating high-difficulty mathematical problems.

2611.32053.title: EffectWAM: Learning Action-Grounded Effects for Robot Manipulation
2611.32053.authors: Yuan Zhang, Hao Cui, Jingfei Ni, Meiyi Wang, Xin Nie, Chi Liu, Wenjie Xu, Lin Gao, Hao Li, Xianhe Zhang, Jiajia Wu, Diyuan Liu, Jia Pan, Chao Ji
2611.32053.abstract: World-action models connect visual prediction with executable robot control. We present EffectWAM, which develops this connection through three complementary components: Effect, camera positional encoding (CaPE), and Action Grounding. Effect represents visual change as the difference between independently encoded future observations and a shared current-observation anchor. CaPE conditions endpoint pooling on relative camera pose when reliable extrinsics are available, while sharing the same learned parameters with pose-free pooling for uncalibrated trajectories. Action Grounding trains the visual representation to retain measured changes in end-effector pose and gripper state. An exponential moving average of the observation encoder supplies Effect targets. A shared generation expert learns to jointly predict Effect and an executable action chunk through flow matching, and reuses the sampled pair to generate future video on demand. This allows the controller to execute actions without waiting for video synthesis. We train on more than 20,000 hours of heterogeneous embodied data, excluding unused chain-of-thought data, and accommodate dataset-specific joint, end-effector, and hand-pose representations. Our evaluation uses the Small (8B) configuration on all five benchmarks and additionally evaluates the Large (26B) configuration on RoboDojo. Experiments examine closed-loop manipulation across complementary benchmarks, and comparisons across multiple baseline policies show consistent improvements from Action Grounding.

2611.32776.title: Learning World Models through Contrastive Identification of Actions
2611.32776.authors: Hayeong Lee, Youngjun Suh, Byung-Jun Lee
2611.32776.abstract: Latent world models enable goal-directed planning from offline visual data, but prediction alone does not specify which action-related distinctions their representations should preserve. Inverse dynamics provides auxiliary supervision, yet squared-error action regression rewards additional information only through changes in the conditional action mean. We propose Contrastive Identification of Actions (CIA), which identifies the executed action among alternatives sampled from a history-conditioned behavior proposal. Comparing actions plausible in the same context targets information supplied by the next latent beyond history. Under exact behavior matching, we show that CIA can reward action information that leaves optimal inverse-regression error unchanged, and verify this distinction through a controlled learning example. CIA achieves higher planner-averaged mean success than the base world model and a regression inverse-dynamics baseline across five visual control benchmarks, without modifying the planner.

2611.32931.title: Reading Decisions Before Spans: Efficient Generative Verification
2611.32931.abstract: A generative verifier can flag an unsupported claim before it finishes describing the error. For applications that only screen an assistant's report, the remaining generation may be unnecessary. We examine this possibility in a frozen 2B span verifier whose output chooses between an empty error list and its first object before producing any locations. Native8 stops at that choice. Prefill1 supplies the seven fixed syntax tokens that precede it and generates just the unrestricted branch token, keeping the native instruction. On 2,015 code-agent TEST responses, Prefill1 uses 84.84% less eager resident service than full generation, with released-reference F1 of 83.43 versus 83.41. It also saves 31.98% over Native8 despite identical logical token totals. This additional saving remains 6.74-26.73% under default compiled execution on the complete workload, with small changes in decisions. Evidence interventions test whether the alarm responds to the supplied facts; first-location decoding measures the additional work and localization losses when a caller also needs an error pointer.

2402.02552.title: Neur2BiLO: Neural Bilevel Optimization
2402.02552.authors: Justin Dumouchelle, Esther Julien, Jannis Kurtz, Elias B. Khalil
2402.02552.abstract: Bilevel optimization deals with nested problems in which a leader takes the first decision to minimize their objective function while accounting for a follower's best-response reaction. Constrained bilevel problems with integer variables are particularly notorious for their hardness. While exact solvers have been proposed for mixed-integer linear bilevel optimization, they tend to scale poorly with problem size and are hard to generalize to the non-linear case. On the other hand, problem-specific algorithms (exact and heuristic) are limited in scope. Under a data-driven setting in which similar instances of a bilevel problem are solved routinely, our proposed framework, Neur2BiLO, embeds a neural network approximation of the leader's or follower's value function, trained via supervised regression, into an easy-to-solve mixed-integer program. Neur2BiLO serves as a heuristic that produces high-quality solutions extremely fast for four applications with linear and non-linear objectives and pure and mixed-integer variables.

2409.00696.title: Polyrating: A Cost-Effective and Bias-Aware Rating System for LLM Evaluation
2409.00696.authors: Jasper Dekoninck, Maximilian Baader, Martin Vechev
2409.00696.abstract: Rating-based human evaluation has become an essential tool to accurately evaluate the impressive performance of large language models (LLMs). However, current rating systems suffer from several important limitations: first, they fail to account for biases that significantly influence evaluation results, second, they require large and expensive preference datasets to obtain accurate ratings, and third, they do not facilitate meaningful comparisons of model ratings across different tasks. To address these issues, we introduce Polyrating, an expressive and flexible rating system based on maximum a posteriori estimation that enables a more nuanced and thorough analysis of model performance at lower costs. Polyrating can detect and quantify biases affecting human preferences, ensuring fairer model comparisons. Further, Polyrating can reduce the cost of human evaluations by up to $59\%$ for new models and up to $77\%$ for new tasks by leveraging existing benchmark scores. Lastly, Polyrating enables direct comparisons of ratings across different tasks, providing a comprehensive understanding of an LLMs' strengths, weaknesses, and relative performance across different applications.

2409.09045.title: United in Diversity? Contextual Biases in LLM-Based Predictions of the 2024 European Parliament Elections
2409.09045.authors: Leah von der Heyde, Anna-Carolina Haensch, Alexander Wenz, Bolei Ma
2409.09045.abstract: "Silicon samples" based on large language models (LLMs) have been argued to serve as efficient alternatives to surveys of humans, assuming that their training data includes information on human attitudes and behavior. However, LLM-generated survey data might exhibit biases, for example due to a lack of diversity in training and alignment processes, which risk reinforcing existing biases in research and policymaking. In this study, we examine to what extent LLM-based predictions of individual public opinion exhibit context-dependent biases by predicting the results of the 2024 EU elections. Before the elections have taken place, we prompt three LLMs with individual-level background information of 26,000 eligible European voters to predict each person's voting behavior. We show that when compared to the actual results, LLM-based predictions of future voting behavior largely fail, their accuracy is unequally distributed across national and linguistic contexts, and they require detailed attitudinal information in the prompt. The findings emphasize the limited applicability of silicon samples to public opinion prediction. In investigating their contextual biases, this study contributes to the understanding and mitigation of inequalities in the development of LLMs and their applications in computational social science.

2503.11006.title: Fine-Grained Instruction-Guided Graph Reasoning for Vision-and-Language Navigation
2503.11006.authors: Yaohua Liu, Binkai Ou, Xinyuan Song, Rong Fu, Amir H. Gandomi, Simon Fong
2503.11006.abstract: Vision and Language Navigation (VLN) requires an embodied agent to traverse complex environments by following natural language instructions, demanding accurate alignment between visual observations and linguistic guidance. To address these challenges, we propose a fine grained instruction guided graph reasoning framework (FIGR) that enhances both spatial representation and instruction understanding during navigation. Specifically, an observation graph interaction mechanism is introduced to disentangle angular and visual cues while strengthening directed edge representations through geometric embedding, enabling more reliable spatial reasoning within the navigation graph. The key detail guidance module is implemented as Adaptive Open Vocabulary Guidance (AOVG), where a contextual role parser dynamically identifies location, object, spatial relation, and other contextual cues. This design avoids exact string matching and supports previously unseen entities and compositional expressions. For multilingual instructions, a Multilingual Semantic Adapter (MSA) maps language-specific representations into a shared navigation-semantic space. By jointly integrating structured graph reasoning with instruction critical semantic cues, the proposed approach significantly improves the agent ability to follow complex navigation instructions. On the validation-unseen splits, FIGR achieves 67 SPL on R2R and 64.8 sDTW on RxR, exceeding SPENav by 1 percentage point in SPL and PRET by 2.4 points in sDTW, respectively.

2504.08207.title: DRAFT-ing Architectural Design Decisions using LLMs
2504.08207.authors: Rudra Dhar, Adyansh Kakran, Amey Karan, Vasudeva Varma, Karthik Vaidhyanathan
2504.08207.abstract: Architectural Knowledge Management (AKM) is crucial for software development and Architectural Decision Records (ADR), an important artifact of AKM, provide a structured approach to capture Architectural Design Decisions (ADD). However, their adoption is limited due to the manual effort involved and insufficient tool support. Prior work shows that LLMs can support ADD generation, though basic prompting yields suboptimal results. This paper explores how LLMs can support architects in two complementary tasks: generating ADDs from Decision Contexts, and generating complete ADRs from titles. We propose Domain-specific Retrieval Augmented Few-shot Tuning (DRAFT), a novel approach that integrates Retrieval Augmented Few-shot Generation with Fine-tuning to generate. DRAFT operates in two phases: an offline phase that fine-tunes a model using retrieval-augmented prompts derived from historical ADRs, and an online phase that generates decisions or complete ADRs by combining retrieved examples with the fine-tuned model. Evaluated on 4344 ADRs across multiple LLMs using standard NLP metrics, DRAFT consistently produces outputs better aligned with real-world ADRs. A human evaluation with the authors and external architects, however, shows no uniformly preferred approach. DRAFT also maintains practical efficiency, reduces dependence- dence on proprietary models, and addresses organizational concerns around privacy, resource constraints, and inference costs.

2504.08604.title: Neural Fidelity Calibration for Informative Sim-to-Real Adaptation
2504.08604.abstract: Deep reinforcement learning can seamlessly transfer agile locomotion and navigation skills from the simulator to real world. However, bridging the sim-to-real gap with domain randomization or adversarial methods often demands expert physics knowledge to ensure policy robustness. Even so, cutting-edge simulators may fall short of capturing every real-world detail, and the reconstructed environment may introduce errors due to various perception uncertainties. To address these challenges, we propose Neural Fidelity Calibration (NFC), a novel framework that employs conditional score-based diffusion models to calibrate simulator physical coefficients and residual fidelity domains online during robot execution. Specifically, the residual fidelity reflects the simulation model shift relative to the real-world dynamics and captures the uncertainty of the perceived environment, enabling us to sample realistic environments under the inferred distribution for policy fine-tuning. Our framework is informative and adaptive in three key ways: (a) we fine-tune the pretrained policy only under anomalous scenarios, (b) we build sequential NFC online with the pretrained NFC's proposal prior, reducing the diffusion model's training burden, and (c) when NFC uncertainty is high and may degrade policy improvement, we leverage optimistic exploration to enable hallucinated policy optimization. Our framework achieves superior simulator calibration precision compared to state-of-the-art methods across diverse robots with high-dimensional parametric spaces. We study the critical contribution of residual fidelity to policy improvement in simulation and real-world experiments. Notably, our approach demonstrates robust robot navigation under challenging real-world conditions, such as a broken wheel axle on snowy surfaces.

2505.12707.title: PLAICraft: Large-Scale Time-Aligned Vision-Speech-Action Dataset for Embodied AI
2505.12707.authors: Yingchen He, Christian D. Weilbach, Martyna E. Wojciechowska, Yiyuan Sun, Jason Yoo, Yuxuan Zhang, Oluwanifemi A. Adekanye, Chia-Hong Hsu, Vasileios Lioutas, Frank Wood
2505.12707.abstract: Advances in deep generative modeling have made it increasingly plausible to train human-level embodied agents. Yet progress has been limited by the absence of large-scale, real-time, multi-modal, and socially interactive datasets that reflect the sensory-motor complexity of natural environments. To address this, we present PLAICraft, a novel data collection platform and dataset capturing multiplayer Minecraft interactions across five time-aligned modalities: video, game output audio, microphone input audio, mouse, and keyboard actions. Each modality is logged with millisecond time precision, enabling the study of synchronous, embodied behaviour in a rich, open-ended world. The dataset comprises 5525 hours of interactive gameplay from more than 232 participants. Alongside the dataset, we provide an evaluation suite for benchmarking model capabilities in object recognition, spatial awareness, language grounding, and long-term memory. PLAICraft opens a path toward training and evaluating agents that act fluently and purposefully in real time, paving the way for truly embodied artificial intelligence.

2506.00058.title: Prompt Engineer: Analyzing Hard and Soft Skill Requirements in the AI Job Market
2506.00058.abstract: The rise of large language models (LLMs) has prompted speculation about a new job role: the prompt engineer. However, empirical evidence on how common such positions are and what skills employers expect of them remains scarce. In this paper, we present a data-driven analysis of a snapshot of LinkedIn job postings for data and AI roles taken in April 2025, after LLMs had entered everyday work but before LLM-based agents became widely adopted. We analyzed 20,662 job postings on LinkedIn for prompt engineers (72 postings) and four established data and AI roles: data scientist, data engineer, data analyst, and machine learning engineer. We find that prompt engineer roles were rare even at this point in time, making up less than 0.5% of the postings across the five roles we sampled. Because our snapshot predates the widespread adoption of LLM-based agents, we argue that the data captures the role of prompt engineer under favorable conditions. Whether its share has since declined is an open question that later snapshots can test. Despite its rarity, prompt engineering has a distinct skill profile. Prompt engineer postings emphasize AI knowledge (22.8%), communication (21.9%), prompt design (18.7%), and creative problem-solving (15.8%). These soft and hard skill requirements differ significantly from those of the four established roles. Taken together, the distinct skill profile and the scarcity of dedicated postings suggest that prompt engineering is best understood not as a profession of its own, but as a distinct skill that is useful across many professions. Our findings inform job seekers, employers, and educators about how to position prompt engineering in the evolving AI workforce.

2506.21621.title: The Open Proof Corpus: A Large-Scale Study of LLM-Generated Mathematical Proofs
2506.21621.authors: Jasper Dekoninck, Ivo Petrov, Kristian Minchev, Mislav Balunovic, Martin Vechev, Miroslav Marinov, Maria Drencheva, Lyuba Konova, Milen Shumanov, Kaloyan Tsvetkov, Nikolay Drenchev, Lazar Todorov, Kalina Nikolova, Nikolay Georgiev, Vanesa Kalinkova, Margulan Ismoldayev
2506.21621.abstract: In recent months, large language models (LLMs) have made significant progress in mathematical proof generation, but further advancement is hindered by the lack of a large-scale, high-quality dataset of human-evaluated proofs. While expensive to create, such a dataset is essential for driving improvements in training and enabling a rigorous analysis of proof generation capabilities. In this work, we present the Open Proof Corpus (OPC), a dataset comprising over 5,000 human-evaluated proofs produced by state-of-the-art LLMs. The OPC was specifically designed for broad applicability and downstream usage in proof generation research and is the first to include a substantial number of correct, LLM-generated solutions to problems from prestigious mathematics competitions such as the USAMO and IMO. Using the OPC, we explore critical questions in automated proof generation: (1) the performance gap between natural language and formal proof generation, (2) the discrepancy between final-answer accuracy and full-proof validity, and (3) the impact of best-of-n selection on proof quality. Finally, to showcase the utility of the OPC, we finetune an 8B-parameter model on the dataset, obtaining a model that performs on par with the best model, Gemini-2.5-Pro, on the task of evaluating proof correctness.

2507.13231.title: VITA: Vision-to-Action Flow Matching Policy
2507.13231.authors: Dechen Gao, Boqi Zhao, Andrew Lee, Ian Chuang, Hanchu Zhou, Hang Wang, Zhe Zhao, Junshan Zhang, Iman Soltani
2507.13231.abstract: Conventional flow matching and diffusion-based policies sample via iterative denoising from standard noise distributions (e.g., Gaussian), and require conditioning modules to repeatedly incorporate visual information during the generative process, incurring substantial time and memory overhead.
